(In the chapter on distance-regular graphs \(f(\theta)\) was a multiplicity; here \(f\) is a form.)

docs.title: Two-way orthogonality forces three families
docs.text:
Collinearity is symmetric, so the form must be reflexive: \(f(v,w) = 0\) exactly when \(f(w,v) = 0\). It should also be nondegenerate, with radical \(0\), since an isotropic vector of the radical would be orthogonal to every point and break (BS2). A \(\sigma\)-sesquilinear form is \((\sigma,\epsilon)\)-Hermitian, for a fixed nonzero scalar \(\epsilon\), if

\[f(w,v) = f(v,w)^\sigma\,\epsilon \quad ext{for all } v, w .\]

For \(\sigma eq 1\), the case \(\epsilon = 1\) is a Hermitian form and the case \(\epsilon = -1\) an anti-Hermitian form. The zero form, which vanishes on every pair of vectors, is called trivial, so a nontrivial form is one that is not identically zero.

Such a form is visibly reflexive. The converse proves the earlier notes' Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem: when \(\dim V \geq 2\), every nondegenerate reflexive form is \((\sigma,\epsilon)\)-Hermitian for some \(\epsilon\). The only subtle part is which side each scalar sits on. Fix \(v\) and compare the maps \(w \mapsto f(v,w)\) and \(w \mapsto f(w,v)^{\sigma^{-1}}\). Both are linear; for the second, \(\sigma^{-1}\) also reverses products, so

\[f(w\lambda, v)^{\sigma^{-1}} = igl(\lambda^\sigma f(w,v) igr)^{\sigma^{-1}} = f(w,v)^{\sigma^{-1}}\lambda .\]

Reflexivity gives them the same kernel, a hyperplane. Two linear functionals on a right vector space with the same kernel differ by a scalar on the left: \(f(w,v)^{\sigma^{-1}} = \gamma_v f(v,w)\). Applying \(\sigma\) reverses the product and moves the scalar to the right: \(f(w,v) = f(v,w)^\sigma \epsilon_v\) with \(\epsilon_v = \gamma_v^\sigma\). For independent \(u\) and \(v\), a vector \(w\) orthogonal to one but not the other (nondegeneracy) gives \(\epsilon_u = \epsilon_{u+v} = \epsilon_v\); dependent vectors are compared through a third, independent one, which is where \(\dim V \geq 2\) is used.

Applying the rule twice to a pair with \(f(v,w) = 1\) gives \(\epsilon^\sigma\epsilon = 1\), and in general shows that \(\sigma^2\) is conjugation by \(\epsilon\); on a field, \(\sigma^2 = 1\).

If \(\sigma = 1\), \(F\) is a field and \(\epsilon = \pm 1\). With \(\epsilon = 1\) the form is symmetric. With \(\epsilon = -1\) outside characteristic 2, \(f(v,v) = -f(v,v)\) forces \(f(v,v) = 0\): alternating. In characteristic 2, \(-1 = 1\), so the form is symmetric, and the alternating forms are the symmetric ones with \(f(v,v) = 0\) for all \(v\).

If \(\sigma eq 1\), rescale. Multiplying \(f\) by a nonzero \(\mu\) keeps orthogonality, so the geometry, but changes the labels: \(\mu f\) is \((\sigma', \epsilon')\)-Hermitian with

\[x^{\sigma'} = \mu\, x^\sigma \mu^{-1}, \qquad \epsilon' = \mu\,(\mu^\sigma)^{-1}\epsilon .\]

A suitable \(\mu\) gives \(\epsilon' = 1\), a Hermitian form with \(\sigma^2 = 1\): over a field, \(\mu = 1 + \epsilon^{-1}\) works when \(\epsilon eq -1\), and \(\mu = a - a^\sigma\), for any \(a\) with \(a^\sigma eq a\), when \(\epsilon = -1\). On a field only \(\epsilon\) moves, but on a skew field rescaling changes \(\sigma\) itself. The form \( ar{v}_0 w_0 + ar{v}_1 w_1\) on \(\mathbb{H}^2\) is Hermitian for conjugation; times \(\mu = i\), its anti-automorphism becomes \(x \mapsto i\, ar{x}\,i^{-1}\), which negates \(i\) but fixes \(j\) and \(k\), and \(\epsilon' = -1\). Neither label is intrinsic; only the family is.

So the funnel has three outlets, the families of the earlier notes: alternating forms (symplectic), symmetric forms (orthogonal) and Hermitian forms (unitary). In characteristic 2 the symmetric outlet is narrow: as the next subsection shows, a trace-valued symmetric form there is alternating, so the bilinear form cannot describe a quadric, and The classical polar spaces uses the quadratic form instead.

docs.title: Why trace-valued forms
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be a nondegenerate \((\sigma,\epsilon)\)-Hermitian form, with the isotropic points as points and the totally isotropic lines as lines; by reflexivity, \(\langle v_1, v_2 angle\) is totally isotropic exactly when \(f(v_1,v_1) = f(v_2,v_2) = f(v_1,v_2) = 0\).

One-or-all is free. For an isotropic point \(x = \langle v angle\) and a totally isotropic line \(L\) not through it, the points \(\langle w angle\) of \(L\) collinear with \(x\) are those with \(f(v,w) = 0\). With \(v\) fixed this is one linear equation on the 2-dimensional space of \(L\), so its solutions are one point or all of \(L\). (BS1) needs only reflexivity and sesquilinearity.

(BS2) needs more. For an isotropic point \(x = \langle v_1 angle\) write \(x^\zeta = \{\langle w angle : f(v_1,w) = 0\}\), the hyperplane of \(\mathrm{PG}(V)\) orthogonal to \(x\). From here on, \(x^\zeta\) always means this hyperplane of the ambient space, non-isotropic points included, and \(x^\perp\) keeps its meaning inside the polar space: the isotropic points of \(x^\zeta\). We need an isotropic point outside \(x^\zeta\). Take \(v_2\) with \(f(v_1,v_2) = 1\) and look for a second isotropic point on \(\langle v_1, v_2 angle\):

\[f(v_2 + v_1\lambda,\; v_2 + v_1\lambda) = f(v_2,v_2) + \epsilon\lambda + \lambda^\sigma .\]

With \( u = -\epsilon\lambda\), the last two terms are \(-( u + u^\sigma\epsilon)\), so a solution exists exactly when \(f(v_2,v_2)\) has the form \( u + u^\sigma\epsilon\). Call \(f\) trace-valued if

\[f(v,v) \in \{ u + u^\sigma\epsilon : u \in F\} \quad ext{for every } v .\]

Over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\) with \(\epsilon = 1\), \( u + u^q\) is the field trace \(T( u)\), hence the name. With this condition every line through \(x\) that leaves \(x^\zeta\) carries a second isotropic point, not collinear with \(x\). So (BS2) holds, the isotropic points span \(\mathrm{PG}(V)\), and \(x^\zeta\) is the tangent hyperplane at \(x\): the lines through \(x\) inside it are tangents or totally isotropic.

The condition usually costs nothing. Outside characteristic 2 it always holds: take \( u = f(v,v)/2\). Over a field with \(\sigma eq 1\) it holds too: after rescaling to \(\epsilon = 1\), \(f(v,v)\) lies in the fixed field of \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda \mapsto \lambda + \lambda^\sigma\) maps onto it. Over fields it bites only in characteristic 2 with \(\sigma = 1\), where \( u + u = 0\), so trace-valued means alternating. Over skew fields of characteristic 2 it is a genuine hypothesis.

Trace-valued is sufficient, not necessary. In characteristic 2, \(f(v+w, v+w) = f(v,v) + f(w,w)\) for a symmetric form, so the isotropic vectors form a subspace, on which \(f\) is alternating, and the geometry is whatever that alternating form gives. The dot product \(\sum v_iw_i\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) is symmetric, nondegenerate and not alternating, and its isotropic vectors are those with \(\sum x_i = 0\).

  • On \(\mathbb{F}_2^4\) they give the 7 points of a plane, only 3 of whose lines are totally isotropic, all through \(j = (1,1,1,1)\). Since \(j\) is orthogonal to every isotropic point, the geometry is a cone and (BS2) fails; the line through \(j\) and \((1,0,0,0)\) leaves \(j^\zeta\) without a second isotropic point.
  • On \(\mathbb{F}_2^5\) they give 15 points, now without \((1,1,1,1,1)\), and the alternating form on them is nondegenerate: its 15 points and 15 totally isotropic lines form the doily.

Two more conditions are needed: isotropic points must exist (the form \(\sum x_iy_i\) on \(\mathbb{R}^4\) has none), and totally isotropic subspaces must be finite-dimensional, as they are when \(V\) is. Then the isotropic points and totally isotropic lines of a nondegenerate trace-valued \((\sigma,\epsilon)\)-Hermitian form form a polar space, whose singular subspaces are the totally isotropic subspaces. When \(\dim V\) is finite, \(f\) also gives a polarity \(U \mapsto U^\zeta\), sending a subspace to the subspace orthogonal to all of it (the earlier notes wrote \(P^\pi\)), and \(U\) is totally isotropic exactly when \(U \subseteq U^\zeta\).

docs.title: Counting isotropic points on a line
docs.text:
The computation above also counts the isotropic points on a line \(\langle v_1, v_2 \rangle\) with both \(v_i\) isotropic and \(f(v_1,v_2) = 1\): they are \(\langle v_1 \rangle\), \(\langle v_2 \rangle\) and the \(\langle v_1 + v_2\kappa \rangle\) with \(\kappa \neq 0\) and \(\kappa + \kappa^\sigma\epsilon = 0\). This one equation gives the three patterns that the earlier notes found family by family.

  • Alternating (\(\sigma = 1\), \(\epsilon = -1\)): \(\kappa - \kappa = 0\) always, so every point of the line is isotropic.
  • Symmetric, characteristic not 2: \(2\kappa = 0\) has no nonzero solution, so the line meets the quadric in 2 points.
  • Hermitian over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\): \(\kappa + \kappa^q = 0\) has \(q-1\) nonzero solutions, so the line has \(q+1\) isotropic points.

For example, the 9-point unital of Designs: a first look, the Hermitian curve \(x_0^3 + x_1^3 + x_2^3 = 0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_4\), meets every line in 1 or \(q + 1 = 3\) points, never all, so it is a polar space of rank 1.

docs.title: Looking from a singular subspace
docs.text:
Quotients are the tool for induction on the rank: The classical polar spaces computes each family's rank by quotienting down to rank 1. Fix a singular subspace \(\alpha\) of dimension \(d \leq n-2\) in a polar space of rank \(n\). The quotient polar space at \(\alpha\) has as points the singular subspaces of dimension \(d+1\) through \(\alpha\). Each singular subspace of dimension \(d+2\) through \(\alpha\) gives a line: the \((d+1)\)-spaces between \(\alpha\) and it. Incidence is containment. For a point, step 2 and the matching below make it a polar space of rank one less; in general we quote that Tits's axioms pass to the quotient, which has rank \(n-1-d\). It is sometimes written \(\Pi_\alpha\) or \(\Pi/\alpha\), and for a point \(x\) often \(x^\perp/x\); the earlier notes called it the residue of \(x\). It is not the internal structure at \(x\) of Point-line geometries, whose points are the points collinear with \(x\). "Quotient" now has three meanings: a quotient vector space, a quotient of an embedding, and this.

The model is step 2's \(a^\perp \cap b^\perp\), isomorphic to the quotient at \(a\) by matching each line through \(a\) with its point collinear with \(b\). So the quotient of the Klein quadric at a point is step 2's grid \(Q^+(3,2)\), and that of the doily is 3 points with no lines.

The quotient is the projection of What projection loses with the centre \(\alpha\) placed on the geometry. Project the points that see all of \(\alpha\) from \(\alpha\): each \((d+1)\)-space through \(\alpha\) collapses to a single point, and what remains is the quotient, the earlier notes' "projecting from the vertex". In coordinates, the quotient at \(\alpha = \mathrm{PG}(U)\) is the polar space of the form induced on the quotient vector space \(U^\zeta/U\) (Linear algebra over finite fields), well defined because \(U\) is orthogonal to all of \(U^\zeta\).

Does the quotient depend on \(\alpha\)? The table at the end of the chapter speaks of "the" rank-1 quotient of a family, so it matters. With at least three points per line and rank at least 2, quotients at singular subspaces of the same dimension are isomorphic. We state this; for points the idea uses step 2: for non-collinear \(a\), \(b\) both quotients are isomorphic to \(a^\perp \cap b^\perp\), and collinear \(x\), \(y\) are joined by non-collinear steps, since a separating point for a third point of \(xy\) sees neither. Thickness matters. In a nonsymmetrical dual grid (Small geometries that test the definitions) with \(k \neq l\) points on its two sides, a point on one side lies on \(l\) lines and a point on the other on \(k\), so their quotients have different sizes.

docs.title: The classical polar spaces
docs.text: Every classical polar space is built the same way, by the earlier notes' Witt decomposition. Peel off hyperbolic pairs, isotropic vectors \(e\), \(e'\) with \(f(e,e') = 1\) (for quadrics, vectors where the quadratic form vanishes), until the rest has no such vector: the anisotropic leftover. The rank is the number of pairs, and peeling a pair is a quotient: with \(a = \langle e \rangle\) and \(b = \langle e' \rangle\), \(a^\perp \cap b^\perp\) is the polar space of the remaining coordinates. Over a finite field the leftover is tiny; over an infinite field it can be large, and in characteristic 2 strange.

docs.title: A finite-field toolkit
docs.text:
From algebra: \(\mathbb{F}_q\) has \(q = p^h\) elements, \(x \mapsto x^p\) is an automorphism (Frobenius), and \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\) has exactly one automorphism of order 2, \(x \mapsto x^q\), fixing \(\mathbb{F}_q\).

  • Squares. For even \(q\), squaring is a bijection, since \(x^2 = y^2\) gives \((x-y)^2 = 0\). For odd \(q\), exactly \((q+1)/2\) elements are squares, counting 0.
  • Trace and norm. On \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\), the field trace is \(T(x) = x + x^q\) and the norm is \(N(x) = x^{q+1}\). Both are fixed by \(x \mapsto x^q\), so they land in \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and both are onto: the norm's kernel on the cyclic group \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*\) has \(q+1\) elements, and the additive trace has a kernel (the roots of \(x^q + x\)) and an image of at most \(q\) elements each, hence exactly \(q\).

The smallest case, \(\mathbb{F}_4\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) with \(\omega^2 = \omega + 1\), shows both maps onto \(\mathbb{F}_2\):

\(x\) \(x^2\) \(T(x) = x + x^2\) \(N(x) = x^3\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(1\) \(1\) \(0\) \(1\) \(\omega\) \(\omega^2\) \(1\) \(1\) \(\omega^2\) \(\omega\) \(1\) \(1\)

The quadric identity. A quadratic form \(\Phi\) (Bilinear and sesquilinear forms in coordinates) has the polar form \(f(v,w) = \Phi(v+w) - \Phi(v) - \Phi(w)\), and

\[\Phi(v + w\lambda) = \Phi(v) + f(v,w)\,\lambda + \Phi(w)\,\lambda^2 .\]

In characteristic 2, \(f(v,v) = 2\Phi(v) = 0\), so the polar form is alternating, as the earlier notes found.

Small forms always have zeros. Every quadratic form in 3 variables over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) vanishes at some nonzero vector, so every conic of \(\mathrm{PG}(2,q)\) has points. For odd \(q\), diagonalize to \(a x_0^2 + b x_1^2 + c x_2^2\); if no coefficient is 0, set \(x_2 = 1\), and the values of \(a x_0^2\) and of \(-c - b x_1^2\) are two sets of \((q+1)/2\) elements of \(\mathbb{F}_q\), so they meet. For even \(q\), the polar form is alternating on a 3-dimensional space, so it has a nonzero radical vector \(v\); on a line \(\langle v, w \rangle\) the identity gives \(\Phi(v + w\lambda) = \Phi(v) + \lambda^2\Phi(w)\), and squaring is onto. Likewise every Hermitian form in 2 variables over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\), diagonalized as \(\lambda_0x_0^{q+1} + \lambda_1x_1^{q+1}\) with \(\lambda_i \in \mathbb{F}_q\), has a zero because the norm is onto. These facts cap the ambient dimension in The classical families side by side.

docs.title: Symplectic polar spaces of every rank
docs.text:
A nondegenerate alternating form lives on a space of even dimension \(2n\) (earlier notes), and a hyperbolic basis \(e_0, \dots, e_{2n-1}\) puts it in the form

\[f(x, y) = (x_0y_1 - x_1y_0) + \dots + (x_{2n-2}y_{2n-1} - x_{2n-1}y_{2n-2}).\]

The polar space is \(W(2n-1,F)\). The points \(a = \langle e_{2n-2} \rangle\) and \(b = \langle e_{2n-1} \rangle\) are not collinear, and \(a^\perp \cap b^\perp\) is the projective space of \(\langle e_0, \dots, e_{2n-3} \rangle\) with a form of the same kind, so the quotient at a point is \(W(2n-3,F)\). Peeling down reaches \(W(1,F)\), a projective line on which \(f\) does not vanish: points but no lines. Hence the rank is \(n\). \(W(2n-1,q)\) has \((q^{2n}-1)/(q-1)\) points; \(W(5,2)\) has 63 points, 315 lines and 135 generators (planes).

Aside: maximal totally isotropic subspaces of \(W(2n-1,2)\) are stabilizer states. Modulo phases, an \(n\)-qubit Pauli \(X^aZ^b\) is a vector \((a,b)\) in \(\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}\), and two Paulis commute exactly when \(a \cdot b' + b \cdot a' = 0\), so the Paulis form \(W(2n-1,2)\), as in the two-qubit aside of Geometries with three points per line. A totally isotropic subspace of vector dimension \(k\) is a commuting set; with signs chosen to exclude \(-I\) it is a stabilizer group, fixing a code space of dimension \(2^{n-k}\). A maximal one has \(k = n\) and fixes a single state, with \(2^n\) sign choices. So the 135 maximal totally isotropic subspaces of \(W(5,2)\) give the 1,080 three-qubit stabilizer states.

docs.title: Quadrics and their tangent hyperplanes
docs.text:
The quadric of \(\Phi\) is the set \(Q\) of points \(\langle v \rangle\) with \(\Phi(v) = 0\). For \(x = \langle v \rangle\) on \(Q\) and another point \(y = \langle w \rangle\), the quadric identity shows that the line \(xy\) meets \(Q\) where \(f(v,w)\lambda + \Phi(w)\lambda^2 = 0\), and at \(y\) if \(\Phi(w) = 0\). So:

  • if \(f(v,w) = 0\) and \(\Phi(w) = 0\), the whole line lies on \(Q\);
  • if \(f(v,w) = 0\) and \(\Phi(w) \neq 0\), the line is a tangent, meeting \(Q\) only in \(x\);
  • if \(f(v,w) \neq 0\), the line meets \(Q\) in exactly two points.

The lines through \(x\) that are tangent or lie on \(Q\) are therefore exactly those in the hyperplane \(x^\zeta = \{\langle w \rangle : f(v,w) = 0\}\): the tangent hyperplane at \(x\) is \(x^\zeta\), and two points of \(Q\) are collinear exactly when they are orthogonal.

The form \(\Phi\) is nondegenerate when no nonzero vector of the radical of \(f\) is singular, that is, has \(\Phi(v) = 0\); the quadric is then called nonsingular: no point of \(Q\) has all its lines on \(Q\) or tangent. "Singular" thus has three uses that do not line up: a singular subspace of a polar space, a singular vector (spanning a point of \(Q\)), and a singular point of a quadric, which is something else again. For nondegenerate \(\Phi\) with points, the three cases give the axioms: one-or-all because \(f(v,w) = 0\) is linear in \(w\), and (BS2) because a line through \(x\) leaving \(x^\zeta\) carries a second point of \(Q\).

docs.title: Families and ranks of quadrics
docs.text:
The largest subspaces on a quadric, or on a Hermitian variety, have some dimension \(n - 1\); this \(n\) is its Witt index, and it is the rank of the polar space. A nonsingular quadric with \(n\) hyperbolic pairs (Witt index \(n\)) and an anisotropic leftover of dimension at most 2 (always the case over finite fields; not over \(\mathbb{R}\)) belongs to one of three families, according as \(\dim V\) is \(2n\), \(2n+1\) or \(2n+2\), with a characteristic-2 variant of the last:

  • hyperbolic, \(Q^+(2n-1,F)\): \(x_0x_1 + \dots + x_{2n-2}x_{2n-1} = 0\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,F)\);
  • parabolic, \(Q(2n,F)\): \(x_0^2 + x_1x_2 + \dots + x_{2n-1}x_{2n} = 0\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(2n,F)\);
  • elliptic, \(Q^-(2n+1,F)\): \(g(x_0,x_1) + x_2x_3 + \dots + x_{2n}x_{2n+1} = 0\) in \(\mathrm{PG}(2n+1,F)\), where \(g\) is an irreducible quadratic form in two variables, such as \(x_0^2 + x_0x_1 + x_1^2\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\). The roots of \(g(X,1)\) generate a quadratic extension \(F'\) and must be distinct (the separable case); the quadric is also written \(Q^-(2n+1, F'/F)\).

Quotienting at a point of the last pair removes the pair, so the ranks come from the bottoms: \(Q^+(1,F)\) is 2 points, \(Q(2,F)\) a conic with \(|F|+1\) points, and \(Q^-(3,F)\) an elliptic quadric with points but no lines. All three have rank 1, so each family has rank \(n\).

Aside: the light cone is an elliptic quadric. At an event, the null vectors \(-t^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 0\) span the light lines, each a future ray \(v\) together with its past ray \(-v\), and as points of \(\mathrm{PG}(3,\mathbb{R})\) they form an elliptic quadric; the slice \(t = 1\) picks one representative of each, giving the sphere \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\), the celestial sphere an observer sees. Two different light lines are never orthogonal, which is why it has points but no lines.

We quote that over finite fields these are all the nonsingular quadrics: in \(\mathrm{PG}(m,q)\) a nonsingular quadric is hyperbolic or elliptic for odd \(m\), parabolic for even \(m\). In rank 3 over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), the Klein quadric \(Q^+(5,2)\) has 35 points, \(Q(6,2)\) has 63, and \(Q^-(7,2)\) has 119. These match the earlier notes' formulas after one translation: their table writes the elliptic quadric as \(Q^-(2n-1,q)\), of rank \(n-1\), so their \(n\) is our \(n+1\).

docs.title: Two families of generators
docs.text:
On the hyperbolic quadric \(Q^+(2n-1,F)\), the quotient at an \((n-2)\)-dimensional singular subspace \(\alpha\) has rank 1 and is \(Q^+(1,F)\): two points. So every \((n-2)\)-dimensional singular subspace lies in exactly two generators, against \(q+1\) for \(W(2n-1,q)\) and \(q^2+1\) for \(Q^-(2n+1,q)\). The two splits the generators into two families, by the rule stated in Projective spaces revisited:

\[M \text{ and } M' \text{ are in the same family} \iff n - 1 - \dim(M \cap M') \text{ is even}.\]

The families are often written \(M_+\) and \(M_-\); for the grid they are the two rulings. They are why the diagram of a hyperbolic quadric branches at its end, and on \(Q^+(7,q)\) they are what triality permutes with the points (earlier notes). The earlier notes stated the rule; here is the proof, in two steps.

  1. Neighbours differ by one. Let \(M_1\), \(M_2\) be the two generators through \(\alpha\), let \(M\) be any generator, and write \(k = \dim(M \cap \alpha)\). Let \(X\) be the set of points of \(M\) that see all of \(\alpha\). Together with \(M \cap \alpha\), some \(n-2-k\) points of \(\alpha\) span \(\alpha\), and each of them sees a hyperplane of \(M\), so \(X\) has dimension at least \((n-1) - (n-2-k) = k+1\). Then \(X\) and \(\alpha\) span a singular subspace bigger than \(\alpha\), which must be \(M_1\) or \(M_2\); say \(M_1\). So \(\dim(M \cap M_1) = k+1\) (no more, since \(\alpha\) is a hyperplane of \(M_1\)). And \(\dim(M \cap M_2) = k\): a point of \(M \cap M_2\) outside \(\alpha\) would see all of \(\alpha\), so lie in \(X \subseteq M_1\), hence in \(M_1 \cap M_2 = \alpha\).
  2. Parity adds up. For generators \(M\), \(M'\), let \(c(M,M') = n - 1 - \dim(M \cap M')\). By the chain fact, \(M\) and \(M'\) are joined by \(c(M,M')\) steps through generators meeting in hyperplanes, and by step 1, for any third generator \(M''\), the dimension of its meet with the current generator changes by one at each step. So \(c(M,M'') \equiv c(M,M') + c(M',M'') \pmod 2\). Even codimension is therefore an equivalence relation, and the two generators through any \(\alpha\) lie in different classes: exactly two families.

On the Klein quadric over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) (\(n = 3\)), the 30 singular planes split 15 and 15. All 210 pairs within a family meet in a point (codimension 2); of the 225 pairs across, 105 meet in a line and 120 are disjoint (codimension 1 and 3, by \(\dim\emptyset = -1\)). In the earlier notes' Klein correspondence one family is the points of \(\mathrm{PG}(3,2)\) and the other its planes, which explains the counts.

docs.title: Pseudo-elliptic quadrics: a characteristic-2 warning
docs.text:
Here is a nondegenerate quadratic form whose polar form has a 2-dimensional radical. It needs a kind of quadratic extension that only characteristic 2 has. An irreducible polynomial is separable if its roots, in the field obtained by adjoining one of them, are distinct, and inseparable otherwise. Outside characteristic 2 every irreducible quadratic is separable, since a double root \(r\) would give \(X^2 - 2rX + r^2\) with \(r\) in the base field. In characteristic 2, \(X^2 + c\) with \(c\) not a square is inseparable: \(X^2 + c = (X + \sqrt{c})^2\). A field of characteristic \(p\) is perfect if every element is a \(p\)-th power (in characteristic 2, a square); fields of characteristic 0 count as perfect. So inseparable quadratics exist exactly over non-perfect fields of characteristic 2, and never over finite fields, where Frobenius is injective and so onto. The quadrics built from an inseparable \(g\) are called pseudo-elliptic quadrics (no relation to the pseudo-quadratic forms of Tits's classification).

To see one, take \(\mathbb{F}_2(t)\), the field of rational functions \(a(t)/b(t)\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\); here \(t\) is a variable, not a quadrangle parameter. It is not perfect: \(t = (a/b)^2\) would give \(t\,b^2 = a^2\), with odd degree on the left and even on the right. Now take

\[\Phi(x) = x_0^2 + t\,x_1^2 + x_2x_3 \quad \text{on } \mathbb{F}_2(t)^4 .\]
  • On \(\langle e_0, e_1 \rangle\), \(x_0^2 + tx_1^2\) is anisotropic, since a nonzero zero would give \(t = (x_0/x_1)^2\).
  • But its polar form is \(2x_0y_0 + 2t\,x_1y_1 = 0\), so the polar form of \(\Phi\) is \(f = x_2y_3 + x_3y_2\), degenerate with radical \(\langle e_0, e_1 \rangle\).
  • Yet \(\Phi\) is nondegenerate, since it is nonzero on the radical outside 0.
  • It has points: \(\langle e_3 \rangle\) and \(\langle (a, b, 1, a^2 + tb^2) \rangle\) for all \(a\), \(b\). The pair \(x_2x_3\) supplies them; \(x_0^2 + tx_1^2\) alone has none.
  • It has no lines. If \(\langle v, w \rangle\) lay on \(Q\), then \(f(v,w) = 0\). In the coordinates \(x_2, x_3\), \(f\) is the nondegenerate alternating form of a plane, where orthogonal vectors are dependent. So a nonzero combination of \(v\) and \(w\) has \(x_2 = x_3 = 0\); it lies in \(\langle e_0, e_1 \rangle\) and on \(Q\), against anisotropy.

So this is a polar space of rank 1, and more hyperbolic pairs give pseudo-elliptic quadrics of any rank. The picture behind it: in characteristic 2 an irreducible \(g = ax_0^2 + bx_0x_1 + cx_1^2\) is separable exactly when it has a cross term, \(b \neq 0\), that is, when its own polar form is nondegenerate. So the radical of the polar form of a nonsingular quadric is 0 for hyperbolic and elliptic quadrics, one point for parabolic ones, and a line for pseudo-elliptic ones.

docs.title: Hermitian varieties and Baer sublines
docs.text:
Let \(\sigma\) be an automorphism of order 2 of a field \(F\), with fixed field \(F_\sigma\) (over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\), \(x \mapsto x^q\) and \(\mathbb{F}_q\)). A Hermitian variety, written \(H\) (not the split Cayley hexagon \(H(2)\)), is the set of points with \(f(v,v) = 0\) for a Hermitian form \(f\), nonsingular when \(f\) is nondegenerate. Hyperbolic pairs give \(H(2n-1, F/F_\sigma)\), with equation \(\sum_{i<n} (x_{2i}x_{2i+1}^\sigma + x_{2i+1}x_{2i}^\sigma) = 0\), and \(H(2n, F/F_\sigma)\), with \(x_0^\sigma x_0 + (x_1x_2^\sigma + x_2x_1^\sigma) + \dots = 0\); over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\) they are \(H(2n-1,q^2)\) and \(H(2n,q^2)\). Both have rank \(n\): peeling off pairs ends at \(H(1, F/F_\sigma)\), a Baer subline, or at \(H(2, F/F_\sigma)\), a curve like \(H(2,4)\), and neither contains a line.

How lines meet. A line through a point \(x\) of the variety lies in the tangent hyperplane \(x^\zeta\) (a tangent or a totally isotropic line) or leaves it. One that leaves it has, by Counting isotropic points on a line, the isotropic points \(\langle v_1 \rangle\), \(\langle v_2 \rangle\) and \(\langle v_1 + v_2\kappa \rangle\) with \(\kappa + \kappa^\sigma = 0\). These \(\kappa\) are \(\kappa_0 c\) for one fixed \(\kappa_0 \neq 0\) and \(c\) in \(F_\sigma\). In the basis \(v_1\), \(v_2\kappa_0\) of the line, the isotropic points are exactly those with coordinates in \(F_\sigma\): a Baer subline, a copy of \(\mathrm{PG}(1,F_\sigma)\), which over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\) is \(q+1\) of the line's \(q^2+1\) points. Since the norm is onto, no line misses \(H(m,q^2)\).

The rest is in the earlier notes: by diagonalization and the onto norm, each \(\mathrm{PG}(m,q^2)\) carries one nonsingular Hermitian variety up to coordinates, \(x_0^{q+1} + \dots + x_m^{q+1} = 0\), and the secants of \(H(2,q^2)\) cut out the unital of Designs: a first look.

docs.title: When symplectic and parabolic coincide
docs.text:
In characteristic 2 the polar form of \(Q(2n,F)\), \(\Phi = x_0^2 + x_1x_2 + \dots + x_{2n-1}x_{2n}\), loses the term \(2x_0y_0\), so its radical is \(\langle e_0 \rangle\), while \(\Phi(e_0) = 1\) keeps \(\Phi\) nondegenerate. This point is the nucleus of What projection loses: it lies on no secant, since \(\Phi(v + e_0\lambda) = \Phi(v) + \lambda^2\) and squaring is injective. On \(\langle e_1, \dots, e_{2n} \rangle\), \(f\) is the form of \(W(2n-1,F)\), and projecting from the nucleus turns one space into the other.

For \(n \geq 2\), \(Q(2n,F) \cong W(2n-1,F)\) exactly when \(F\) is a perfect field of characteristic 2. (For \(n = 1\) both are sets of \(|F|+1\) points with no lines, isomorphic over every field.) Why perfect characteristic 2 suffices: let \(\theta\) drop \(x_0\), the projection from the nucleus.

  • On points: \((x_1, \dots, x_{2n})\) comes from a point of the quadric exactly when \(x_0^2 = x_1x_2 + \dots + x_{2n-1}x_{2n}\) is solvable. A square root is unique in characteristic 2 when it exists, so \(\theta\) is injective, and it is onto exactly when every element is a square.
  • On collinearity: two points of the quadric are collinear exactly when \(f(v,w) = 0\), and \(f(v,w) = f(\theta v, \theta w)\), which is collinearity in \(W(2n-1,F)\).

So for perfect \(F\), \(\theta\) is a bijection of points under which two points are collinear exactly when their images are, and since the point graph determines the polar space, it is an isomorphism; over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), the doily is both \(W(3,2)\) and \(Q(4,2)\). Over \(\mathbb{F}_2(t)\), \(\theta\) misses the point \(\langle e_1 + e_2t \rangle\), which would need \(x_0^2 = t\); that no isomorphism exists at all is the converse, which we quote (it compares which pairs of disjoint lines lie in a grid). For odd \(q\) there is no nucleus, and \(W(3,q)\) and \(Q(4,q)\) are dual but not isomorphic (Generalized quadrangles in depth).

docs.title: The classical families side by side
docs.text:
How big is the ambient space? The toolkit's two facts cap it, as the earlier notes found through the Witt decomposition and the Chevalley–Warning theorem. Directly: if a nonsingular quadric of rank \(n\) lay in \(\mathrm{PG}(m,q)\) with \(m \geq 2n+2\), the vectors orthogonal to a generator \(W\) would leave room for a 3-dimensional subspace meeting \(W\) only in 0; it contains a singular vector, which would extend \(W\). So \(m \in \{2n-1, 2n, 2n+1\}\), and a 2-dimensional subspace gives \(m \in \{2n-1, 2n\}\) for nonsingular Hermitian varieties.

Names. The polar space of a hyperbolic quadric \(Q^+(2n-1,F)\) is called a hyperbolic polar space, that of a parabolic quadric \(Q(2n,F)\) a parabolic polar space, and that of an elliptic quadric \(Q^-(2n+1,F)\) an elliptic polar space, or a pseudo-elliptic polar space in the inseparable case. A Hermitian variety gives a Hermitian polar space, and \(W(2n-1,F)\) is the symplectic polar space.

In the table, the rank-1 base is the quotient at a next-to-maximal, \((n-2)\)-dimensional, singular subspace. Its size is the number of generators through such a subspace, the earlier notes' \(q^e + 1\) (with \(q^2\) in place of \(q\) for the Hermitian rows), and for \(n = 2\) it is \(t+1\), the number of lines on a point; so the order column recovers the table of Generalized quadrangles in depth.

Family Ambient space Rank-1 base (size) Quadrangle order \((s,t)\) Smallest rank 3 In characteristic 2 \(Q^+(2n-1,q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,q)\) \(Q^+(1,q)\) (2) \((q,1)\) \(Q^+(5,2)\): 35 points polar form nondegenerate alternating \(W(2n-1,q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(1,q)\) (\(q+1\)) \((q,q)\) \(W(5,2)\): 63 points isomorphic to \(Q(2n,q)\) \(Q(2n,q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(2n,q)\) conic \(Q(2,q)\) (\(q+1\)) \((q,q)\) \(Q(6,2)\): 63 points nucleus; isomorphic to \(W(2n-1,q)\) \(Q^-(2n+1,q)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(2n+1,q)\) \(Q^-(3,q)\) (\(q^2+1\)) \((q,q^2)\) \(Q^-(7,2)\): 119 points polar form nondegenerate alternating \(H(2n-1,q^2)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(2n-1,q^2)\) Baer subline (\(q+1\)) \((q^2,q)\) \(H(5,4)\): 693 points nothing special \(H(2n,q^2)\) \(\mathrm{PG}(2n,q^2)\) \(H(2,q^2)\) (\(q^3+1\)) \((q^2,q^3)\) \(H(6,4)\): 2,709 points nothing special

Hermitian spaces need a field of square order; the others exist over every finite field. Read down the third column: each classical polar space is a stack of hyperbolic pairs on its rank-1 base, whose size is \(t+1\) for every rank-2 quotient in the stack, while \(s+1\) comes from the field.

In short. Characteristic 2 is where the classical families touch. The polar form of every quadric is alternating there, so a symmetric bilinear form that passes the trace-valued test cannot describe a quadric, and the quadratic form takes over. The radical of that polar form measures how far the quadric is from its symplectic shadow: zero for hyperbolic and elliptic quadrics, the nucleus for parabolic ones, a line for pseudo-elliptic ones. Square roots settle the rest. Over a perfect field, every finite field included, the nucleus projects \(Q(2n)\) onto \(W(2n-1)\) and no pseudo-elliptic quadric exists; over \(\mathbb{F}_2(t)\) both fail.

docs.title: Designs
docs.text:
In the gallery, a design was what remains of a geometry once everything but uniform counts is forgotten: \(v\) points, blocks of \(k\) points, and every \(t\) points on exactly \(\lambda\) blocks. The \(2\)-designs with \(k < v\) are the balanced incomplete block designs, or BIBDs, of the earlier projective geometry notes. How much can the counts force on their own? If every \(t\) points lie on \(\lambda\) blocks, do every \(s < t\) points, and every single point, also lie on a constant number of blocks? Which parameter sets are impossible? And can a design have fewer blocks than points?

The first two questions yield to counting one set in two ways. The third needs linear algebra, the move we made for strongly regular graphs: turn the counts into an equation for a matrix, then read off its eigenvalues. There the multiplicities had to be whole numbers and had to leave room for one vector per vertex. Here a matrix will have to leave room for one vector per point, and that forces enough blocks.

Three letters carry over from earlier chapters with new meanings. Here \(\lambda\) is the design's count, not the \(\lambda\) of a strongly regular graph; \(k\) is the block size, not a valency; and \(t\), together with the \(s\) about to appear, is a strength, not part of an order \((s, t)\). As in the gallery, \(q\) is the order of a plane.

docs.title: Every t-design is an s-design
docs.text:
If every \(3\) points of a design lie on \(\lambda\) blocks, must every \(2\) points lie on the same number of blocks? Nothing in the definition says so. Yet it is true, and one argument handles every smaller strength: a \(t\)-\((v, k, \lambda)\) design is also an \(s\)-design for every \(s\) with \(1 \leq s \leq t\), meaning that every \(s\) points lie on a constant number \(\lambda_s\) of blocks.

Counting one set in two ways. Fix a set \(X\) of \(s\) points, and count the pairs \((Y, B)\) in which \(B\) is a block and \(Y\) is a set of \(t\) points with \(X \subseteq Y \subseteq B\).

  • Choose \(Y\) first. It is \(X\) together with \(t - s\) of the other \(v - s\) points, so there are \(\binom{v-s}{t-s}\) choices, and each \(Y\) lies in exactly \(\lambda\) blocks.
  • Choose \(B\) first. Say \(\lambda_X\) blocks contain \(X\). Inside each, \(Y\) is \(X\) together with \(t - s\) of the other \(k - s\) points of the block, so there are \(\binom{k-s}{t-s}\) choices.

The two counts agree, so

\[\lambda_X = \lambda_s = \lambda \, \frac{\binom{v-s}{t-s}}{\binom{k-s}{t-s}},\]

which does not depend on which \(s\) points we chose. With \(s = 1\), every point lies on the same number \(r = \lambda_1\) of blocks, the replication number (the earlier notes' point replication). By convention \(\lambda_0 = b\), the number of blocks, which is the formula with \(X\) empty and the count met in the gallery. Counting incident point-block pairs once by points and once by blocks gives

\[bk = vr,\]

and for a \(2\)-design the formula with \(s = 1\) reads \(r(k - 1) = \lambda(v - 1)\): the earlier notes' two fundamental necessary conditions. For the Fano plane, \(r = 6/2 = 3\) and \(b = 21/3 = 7\).

A closed form. The formula gives \(\lambda_{t-1} = \lambda (v-t+1)/(k-t+1)\), so

\[\lambda_{t-1} - \lambda = \lambda \, \frac{v - k}{k - t + 1}, \qquad \text{and for } t = 2, \qquad r - \lambda = \lambda \, \frac{v - k}{k - 1}.\]

So \(r > \lambda\) exactly when \(v > k\), when no block contains every point. This one fact is used twice below.

The formula builds parameters. Suppose an \(S(5, 8, 24)\) exists, as the gallery quoted. Then every count is fixed:

\(s\) \(5\) \(4\) \(3\) \(2\) \(1\) \(0\) \(\lambda_s\) \(1\) \(5\) \(21\) \(77\) \(253\) \(759\)

Since \(\lambda_s\) counts the blocks through \(s\) fixed points, it is the number of blocks of the design derived \(s\) times, so the table reproduces the gallery's chain \(759, 253, 77, 21\).

The formula kills candidates. Every \(\lambda_s\) must be a whole number. Try an \(S(3, 4, 17)\). Its block count \(b = \binom{17}{3} / \binom{4}{3} = 170\) is whole, and so is \(r = \binom{16}{2} / \binom{3}{2} = 40\), but

\[\lambda_2 = \frac{\binom{15}{1}}{\binom{2}{1}} = \frac{15}{2},\]

so no such design exists: the refined counts see what the block count alone misses. The same formula gave the fractional \(126/5\) that, in the gallery, stopped the Fano plane's extension \(S(3, 4, 8)\) from extending again. Integrality is necessary, not sufficient. A projective plane of order \(6\) would be an \(S(2, 7, 43)\), with \(r = 7\) and \(b = 43\), both whole; yet the Bruck–Ryser theorem rules it out (the aside on plane orders).

For planes, the counts force the axioms. For \(q \geq 2\), the Steiner systems \(S(2, q+1, q^2+q+1)\) are exactly the projective planes of order \(q\), and the \(S(2, q, q^2)\) are exactly the affine planes of order \(q\). One direction is counting a plane's points. For the other, a Steiner system with \(t = 2\) is a linear space with lines of fixed size, so only the plane axioms need checking.

  • In an \(S(2, q+1, q^2+q+1)\), each point lies on \(r = (q^2 + q)/q = q + 1\) lines. Take two distinct lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), and a point \(x\) on \(L_2\) but not on \(L_1\). Joining \(x\) to the \(q + 1\) points of \(L_1\) gives \(q + 1\) lines through \(x\), all different, since a line through \(x\) and two points of \(L_1\) would be \(L_1\). These are all the lines through \(x\), so \(L_2\) is one of them and meets \(L_1\). Every line has \(q + 1 \geq 3\) points, so the plane is no near-pencil: it is nondegenerate.
  • In an \(S(2, q, q^2)\), each point lies on \(r = (q^2 - 1)/(q - 1) = q + 1\) lines. For a point \(x\) off a line \(L\), exactly \(q\) of them meet \(L\), one through each point of \(L\), which leaves exactly one line through \(x\) that misses \(L\): the parallel axiom.

In both cases \(r \geq 2\) gives two lines through a point, hence three non-collinear points. No coordinates were needed: the counts alone build the plane. The gallery ran the affine argument for the 9-point unital, and relied on it for the derived designs of inversive planes.

The lesson of this section: one formula builds all the parameters of a design from \((t, v, k, \lambda)\), and its fractions kill candidates.

docs.title: New designs from old
docs.text:
The gallery's derived design at a point \(x\) keeps the blocks through \(x\), with \(x\) removed (derived designs and extensions). Two more constructions use the other blocks, or swap "in" for "out". One example will show all three at work.

The external structure. Keep instead the blocks that miss \(x\), on the points other than \(x\). This is the external structure at \(x\), also called the residual design. For a \(t\)-\((v, k, \lambda)\) design with \(t \geq 2\) and \(v > k\) it is a \((t-1)\)-\((v-1, k, \lambda_{t-1} - \lambda)\) design: \(t - 1\) points other than \(x\) lie on \(\lambda_{t-1}\) blocks, and \(\lambda\) of these also contain \(x\). By the closed form, \(\lambda_{t-1} - \lambda\) is positive exactly when \(v > k\). If \(v = k\) the design is a single block containing every point, and no block misses \(x\).

The complementary design. Keep all the points of a design \(\mathcal{S}\) and replace each block \(B\) by its complement \(\mathcal{P} \setminus B\). For a \(2\)-\((v, k, \lambda)\) design with \(v - k \geq 2\), the result is the complementary design \(\overline{\mathcal{S}}\), a \(2\)-\((v, v-k, b - 2r + \lambda)\) design. Two points \(x_1, x_2\) lie in the complement of \(B\) exactly when \(B\) contains neither. Of the \(b\) blocks, \(r\) contain \(x_1\), \(r\) contain \(x_2\) and \(\lambda\) contain both, so

\[b - (r + r - \lambda) = b - 2r + \lambda\]

blocks contain neither, the same number for every pair. The hypothesis \(v - k \geq 2\) gives the new blocks at least two points, and makes the number positive, since two points outside one block lie together in its complement. (Complements of \(t\)-designs are \(t\)-designs too, by inclusion and exclusion, but we need only \(t = 2\).) The complementary design is not the dual: the dual swaps points and blocks, while the complement keeps both and swaps "in" for "out", as the complement of a graph swaps edges for non-edges.

Example: one design, three constructions. Take the gallery's \(S(3, 4, 8)\), the \(14\) planes of \(AG(3, 2)\), each point on \(r = 7\) of them, and fix a point \(x\).

  • The derived design at \(x\) is the Fano plane: the \(7\) planes through \(x\), minus \(x\), are its lines.
  • The external structure at \(x\) keeps the \(7\) planes that miss \(x\). By the closed form it is a \(2\)-\((7, 4, 2)\) design, since \(\lambda_2 - \lambda = 1 \cdot (8 - 4)/(4 - 3 + 1) = 2\).
  • These \(7\) planes are exactly the complements, among the other \(7\) points, of the Fano lines: each plane through \(x\) has a parallel plane missing \(x\), and the two partition \(\mathbb{F}_2^3\). So the external structure is the complementary design of the derived one. The parameters agree: for the Fano plane, \(b - 2r + \lambda = 7 - 6 + 1 = 2\).

Deriving and taking the external structure lower the strength, from \(3\) to \(2\); complementing keeps it.

Aside: the complementary Fano design is the Steane code. Label the Fano points so that its lines are the supports of the weight-3 words of the \([7, 4]\) Hamming code. The complements of the lines, the blocks of the \(2\)-\((7, 4, 2)\) design, are then the supports of the \(7\) nonzero words of the dual \([7, 3]\) simplex code, spanned by the Hamming code's parity checks. The Steane code uses exactly these supports for both its \(X\)-type and its \(Z\)-type stabilizers. Any two blocks of the complementary design meet in exactly \(2\) points, an even number, and that is why every \(X\)-type stabilizer commutes with every \(Z\)-type one.

A look back. Deriving is a cousin of the quotient polar space at a point, not the same construction. Both stand at a point \(x\) and keep what passes through it, and both lower the key parameter by one: the strength of a design, the rank of a polar space. They differ in what becomes a point. The derived design keeps the old points, while the points of the quotient are the lines through \(x\). Repeated deriving runs the gallery's Witt chains down to planes, and repeated quotients compute the ranks of the classical polar spaces.

docs.title: Fisher's inequality
docs.text:
A projective plane has as many lines as points, and an affine plane more: \(AG(2, 3)\) has \(12\) lines on \(9\) points. Can a \(2\)-design have fewer blocks than points? Counting does not seem to forbid it. Room does.

The incidence matrix of a 2-design. Let \(M\) be the incidence matrix of a \(2\)-\((v, k, \lambda)\) design, as in the first chapter: rows for points, columns for blocks, real entries \(0\) and \(1\). The entry of \(MM^T\) in row \(x\) and column \(y\) counts the blocks containing both \(x\) and \(y\): \(r\) when \(x = y\), and \(\lambda\) otherwise. So

\[MM^T = (r - \lambda) I + \lambda J,\]

the first chapter's Fano computation \(2I + J\), now for every \(2\)-design.

Its eigenvalues. A \(v \times v\) matrix \(\alpha I + \beta J\) (Greek letters, since \(b\) now counts blocks) has eigenvalue \(\alpha + v\beta\) on the all-ones vector \(j\) and eigenvalue \(\alpha\) on the \((v-1)\)-dimensional space \(j^\perp\), where \(J\) acts as zero (the all-ones matrix). As for strongly regular graphs, the \(J\) term drops out on \(j^\perp\). So \(MM^T\) has the eigenvalue \(r + (v-1)\lambda\) once, and \(r - \lambda\) with multiplicity \(v - 1\). The first equals \(rk\), by \(r(k-1) = \lambda(v-1)\); it is the row sum of \(MM^T\), since a point lies on \(r\) blocks of \(k\) points each. For the Fano plane the eigenvalues are \(9 = 3 \cdot 3\) once and \(2\) six times; for \(AG(2, 3)\), with \(r = 4\) and \(\lambda = 1\), they are \(12 = 4 \cdot 3\) once and \(3\) eight times.

Room for every point. If \(v > k\), the closed form gives \(r - \lambda > 0\), so both eigenvalues are positive and \(MM^T\) is invertible, of rank \(v\). Over the reals \(\operatorname{rank} M = \operatorname{rank} MM^T\) (rank, determinants and Gram matrices). So \(M\) has rank \(v\), and a matrix with \(v\) independent rows needs at least \(v\) columns. This is Fisher's inequality: a \(2\)-\((v, k, \lambda)\) design with \(v > k\) has

\[b \geq v,\]

at least as many blocks as points. It is a test of room, like the absolute bound for strongly regular graphs. \(MM^T\) is the Gram matrix of the rows of \(M\), one vector in \(\mathbb{R}^b\) for each point; the vectors are independent, so \(\mathbb{R}^b\) must have room for all \(v\) of them, just as an eigenspace had to have room for one vector per vertex. Since \(bk = vr\), the inequality also says \(r \geq k\): a point lies on at least as many blocks as a block has points. The hypothesis \(v > k\) is the "incomplete" in the earlier notes' BIBD.

What each hypothesis does.

  • Strength \(2\) makes all the off-diagonal entries of \(MM^T\) equal. With strength \(1\) the inequality fails: the derived design of the Fano plane, three disjoint pairs covering \(6\) points, is a \(1\)-\((6, 2, 1)\) design with only \(3\) blocks, and its \(MM^T\) has rank \(3\).
  • \(v > k\) gives \(r > \lambda\). Without it, a single block containing all \(v\) points is a \(2\)-\((v, v, 1)\) design with \(b = 1\); here \(r = \lambda = 1\), so \(MM^T = J\), of rank \(1\).

Equality: symmetric designs. The Fano plane meets the bound, \(b = v = 7\), and so does every projective plane, \(b = v = q^2 + q + 1\). So do the earlier notes' point-hyperplane designs of \(PG(n, q)\), such as the points and planes of \(PG(3, 2)\), a \(2\)-\((15, 7, 3)\) design, and the \(2\)-\((7, 4, 2)\) design of the Steane aside. The earlier notes called these symmetric BIBDs: \(b = v\), or equivalently \(r = k\), by \(bk = vr\). An affine plane of order \(q\) falls short of equality, with \(q^2 + q\) lines on \(q^2\) points. Symmetric designs have a theory of their own, beyond these notes, which is where the Bruck–Ryser theorem is proved. Its starting point is visible in the examples: any two blocks meet in exactly \(\lambda\) points, as two planes of \(PG(3, 2)\) meet in a line of \(3\) points, so the dual of a symmetric design is again a \(2\)-design with the same parameters.

The opening questions, answered. Every \(s \leq t\) points lie on exactly \(\lambda_s\) blocks, a number fixed by \((t, v, k, \lambda)\); in particular every point lies on \(r\) blocks. A parameter set is impossible if some \(\lambda_s\) is a fraction, as for \(S(3, 4, 17)\). And a \(2\)-design with \(v > k\) never has fewer blocks than points. Passing these tests builds nothing for one parameter set, as order \(6\) shows. In bulk, though, it is enough: Keevash (2014) proved that for fixed \(t\), \(k\) and \(\lambda\), designs exist for every large enough \(v\) whose \(\lambda_s\) are all whole numbers.

In short. Four kinds of test have run through these notes. Counting: the same set counted two ways, as in \(bk = vr\) and in the counting identity for strongly regular graphs. Integrality: counts and dimensions are whole numbers, here the \(\lambda_s\), there the eigenvalue multiplicities. Room: independent vectors need enough dimensions, here Fisher's \(b \geq v\), there the absolute bound. Positivity: entrywise products of projectors stay positive semidefinite, the Krein conditions for graphs. None of the tests builds anything, but together they decide which parameter sets are worth looking for.

This ends our tour of incidence geometry. Later chapters of these notes will turn to the classical groups, the symmetry groups of the projective and polar spaces met here.

docs.title: Probability & States
docs.text:
A system usually has several different states it can inhabit. These states are called microstates. Microstates that are indistinguishable from each other are clubbed under a single macrostate, and the number of microstates that make up a macrostate is called the multiplicity of that macrostate.

For eg. if we have 100 coins, there is only one way in which every coin will be heads up. i.e. the macrostate of all coins being heads up has a multiplicity of 1. However, the macrostate of one coin being heads up and the rest tails up has a multiplicity of 100 because any one of the 100 coins could be heads up, and each of these represents a different microstate.

If we assume that every microstate is equally probable, a system is most likely to eventually end up in the macrostate with the highest multiplicity i.e. the most probable macrostate. The probability of this occurring is given by:

\[\frac{\Omega_{\text{max}}}{\Omega_{\text{total}}}\]

where \(\Omega\) is the multiplicity.

For the coin example, this works out to \(\frac{\binom{N}{N/2}}{2^N}\), where \(N\) is the number of coins. To evaluate this, we can use the Stirling approximation for \(N!\), which is given by \(\left(\frac{N}{e}\right)^N\sqrt{2\pi N}\).

Aside: To understand how the Stirling formula works, consider that \(N!\) contains a product of \(N\) numbers, which in the Stirling approximation is represented by \(N^N\). Of course, this would mean we are overcounting quite a bit and so we "average" out the numbers by dividing each \(N\) by \(e\). Thus we get \(\left(\frac{N}{e}\right)^N\). But this is too much of a correction and so we multiply the \(\sqrt{2\pi N}\) term.

Using the Stirling approximation, we see that:

\[\frac{\binom{N}{N/2}}{2^N} \approx \frac{\left(\frac{N}{e}\right)^N \sqrt{2\pi N}}{\left(\left(\frac{N}{2e}\right)^{N/2} \sqrt{\pi N}\right)^2 2^N}\]

Cancelling out the terms, we get the final value as: $\(\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi N}}\)$

This is the probability of a system ending up in its most probable state. The probability decreases as \(N\) increases. However, though the probability of ending up in the most probable state goes down, the probability of ending up in the neighbourhood of the most probable state rises.

We can illustrate this by considering a system of \(N\) particles that can have \(q\) energy states distributed among them. Assume that \(q \gg N\). The total multiplicity of all states is

\[\Omega(N,q) = \binom{q+N-1}{q} = \frac{(q+N-1)!}{q!(N-1)!} \approx \frac{(q+N)!}{q!N!}\] \[\begin{aligned} \ln \Omega &= \ln \left( \frac{(q+N)!}{q! N!} \right) \\ &= \ln(q+N)! - \ln q! - \ln N! \\ &\approx (q+N)\ln(q+N) - (q+N) - q\ln q + q - N\ln N + N \\ &= (q+N)\ln(q+N) - q\ln q - N\ln N \end{aligned}\] \[\begin{aligned} \ln(q+N) &= \ln \left[ q\left(1 + \frac{N}{q}\right) \right] \\ &= \ln q + \ln\left(1 + \frac{N}{q}\right) \\ &\approx \ln q + \frac{N}{q} \end{aligned}\]

Taking the Taylor explansion: \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) for \(\vert{}x\vert{} \ll 1\)

\[\ln \Omega \approx N \ln \frac{q}{N} + N + \frac{N^2}{q}\]

At the limit \(q \gg N\)

\[\Omega(N,q) \approx e^{N \ln(q/N)} e^N = \left(\frac{eq}{N}\right)^N\]

Now imagine that there were two systems, each with \(N\) particles and \(q_A\) and \(q_B\) energy states each, and we'd like to see what the odds are of the systems settling into the most likely state of \(q_A = q_B\).

\[\Omega_{\text{max}} = \left(\frac{e}{N}\right)^{2N} \left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^{2N}\]

To see what the multiplicity is like a little away from this peak, we set:

\[q_A = \frac{q}{2} + x, \quad q_B = \frac{q}{2} - x\] \[\Omega = \left(\frac{e}{N}\right)^{2N} \left[ \left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^2 - x^2 \right]^N\] \[\begin{aligned} \ln\left[ \left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^2 - x^2 \right]^N &= N \ln\left[ \left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^2 - x^2 \right] \\ &= N \ln\left[ \left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^2 \left( 1 - \left(\frac{2x}{q}\right)^2 \right) \right] \\ &= N \left[ \ln\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^2 + \ln\left(1 - \left(\frac{2x}{q}\right)^2\right) \right] \\ &\approx N \left[ \ln\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{2x}{q}\right)^2 \right] \end{aligned}\] \[\Omega = \left(\frac{e}{N}\right)^{2N} e^{N \ln(q/2)^2} e^{-N(2x/q)^2} = \Omega_{\text{max}} \cdot e^{-N(2x/q)^2}\]

This is a typical Gaussian distribution and drops off by \(1/e\) at

\[N \left(\frac{2x}{q}\right)^2 = 1 \quad \text{or} \quad x = \frac{q}{2\sqrt{N}}\]

\(\frac{q}{2\sqrt{N}}\) will be a very large number, but compared to the most probable state of \(\frac{q}{2}\), it is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\) time smaller. For even a small macroscopic system, \(N\) will be of the order of \(10^{23}\) or more. Because the relative width of this Gaussian distribution scales as \(1/\sqrt{N}\), the width of the peak is barely a hundred-billionth of the total possible range of states. This means that the system is overwhelmingly likely to end up in a state microscopically close and macroscopically indistinguishable from the most probable state due to sheer probability, making macroscopic fluctuations away from equilibrium effectively impossible.

Even if a system starts off in its most improbable state, it will invariably move towards the more probable states because there are exponentially more transitions leading to more probable states than there are transitions leading to less probable states. Eventually, the system must end up in its most probable neighbourhood.

This is the statistical interpretation of the second law of thermodynamics. While classical thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system (like the universe) can never decrease, statistical mechanics frames this as the system overwhelmingly tending to evolve toward its most probable macrostate. Macroscopic decreases in entropy are theoretically possible but statistically so improbable that they are never observed.

docs.title: Intensive & Extensive Properties
docs.text:
In thermodynamics, properties are classified based on how they change with the size or amount of matter in a system. Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of substance (e.g., temperature, pressure, density), while extensive properties scale with the size of the system (e.g., mass, volume, total energy). Their values add up when subsystems combine.

\(T\), \(P\), \(\rho\) are intensive. \(m\), \(V\), \(U\), enthalpy \(H\), entropy \(S\), and both Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies, \(F\) and \(G\), are extensive.

Key Rules: You can add or subtract between properties of the same class (provided their physical units match), but you cannot mix intensive and extensive properties in addition/subtraction.

Multiplying an intensive and extensive property gives another extensive property.

Dividing two extensive properties yields an intensive property.

docs.title: State & Non-state Variables
docs.text:
State variables are independent of the process or path taken in state space to traverse between two states. They depend only on the initial and final states. \(U\), \(H\), \(S\), \(F\), \(G\), \(T\), \(P\), \(V\) are state variables. The cyclic integral of the differential of a state variable over a closed path in state space is always zero (e.g., \(\oint dU = 0\)).

Non-state variables depend on how the final state was arrived at. \(Q\) and \(W\) are non-state variables, which is why we represent them with inexact differentials (\(\delta Q\), \(\delta W\)), representing an infinitesimal amount of energy transferred along a specific path in state space. If you went from state \(A\) to \(B\) via a reversible process compared to a non-reversible process, both the total \(\int \delta Q\) and \(\int \delta W\) would be different.

docs.title: Entropy
docs.text:
The entropy of a system in equilibrium, where every accessible microstate is equally probable, is given by Boltzmann's entropy formula:

\[S = k_B \ln\Omega\]

For a system where microstates have varying probabilities, the general form (Gibbs entropy) is used:

\[S = -k_B \sum_s P_s \ln P_s\]

If we take the \(k_B\) out of this formula and make it dimensionless, it is called the Shannon Entropy formula and is used in Information Theory. In this context, the logarithm is typically taken to base 2, and the resulting entropy is measured in "bits".

If \(P_s\) is equal for all accessible microstates, then \(P_s = \frac{1}{\Omega}\) for every state, and Boltzmann's and Gibb's formulations become identical. You can check this by substituting \(P_s\) with \(\Omega\) into the summation gives:

\[-k_B \sum_s \left( \frac{1}{\Omega} \ln\frac{1}{\Omega} \right) = -k_B \sum_s \left( \frac{1}{\Omega} (-\ln\Omega) \right) = k_B \sum_s \left( \frac{1}{\Omega} \ln\Omega \right)\]

Since the sum is taken over all \(\Omega\) states, the summation evaluates to \(\Omega\) identical terms. This \(\Omega\) cancels the \(\frac{1}{\Omega}\) factor, yielding the original formula for equilibrium entropy.

In Short: When working with a system that has not yet reached equilibrium, we need to determine which states are more likely. We therefore calculate the entropy of various states using the multiplicities of those states to determine the final likely state i.e. the one with highest entropy. Once equilibrium is reached, the entropy of the system is given by the total multiplicity of all possible states, not just the most probable states. However, even if we do make our entropy calculations with the multiplicity of the most probable state, it is unlikely to be off by much because the total multiplicity is approximately the multiplicity of the most probable state.

Aside: In Information Theory, entropy is related to the "usefulness" or "surprise" of information. To understand this, consider asking for someone's birthday, and receiving one of the following answers: 1. "Sometime this year" (probability \(P=1\)) 2. "It is in January" (probability \(P \approx 1/12\)) 3. "It is on the 11th of a month" (probability \(P \approx 12/365\))

The first statement is essentially useless and carries zero surprise, but has a probability of 1. The third statement is highly specific, has a much lower probability of being guessed randomly, and thus provides a high amount of information when revealed. The information content (or surprisal) of a specific outcome is proportional to \(-\log_2 P\). The more improbable a piece of information, the more it helps constrain the uncertainty in information.

However, a highly improbable outcome, while carrying immense information value, occurs rarely. In information theory, we therefore define entropy as the uncertainty of the system. The more information we get from an improbable piece of content, the more we constrain the uncertainty. However, this improbable event is highly unlikely to take place. So we calculate the expected value of the information: \(S = -\sum_s P_s \ln P_s\)

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text:
Previously, we considered two systems, each with \(N\) particles and \(q_A\) and \(q_B\) energy states each. We saw that the two systems are highly likely to reach an equilibrium where they share the energy almost equally. If the energy was in the form of heat, we could just as well have said the two systems are extremely likely to end up at the same temperature. Temperature therefore is not defined as a fundamental quantity but as the heat (along a reversible path between states \(A\) and \(B\)) required for a unit change in entropy:

\[T = \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{dS}\]

and therefore:

\[dS = \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}\]

This is the second law of thermodynamics.

When a process does not cause a change in volume or the number of particles in the system, the change in the system's energy \(dU= \delta Q_{\text{rev}}\) and so \(\frac{1}{T} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\).

If more heat is required to change entropy, the system is at a higher temperature.

The other way to look at this is: a high temperature system will not lose much entropy for a large loss of heat. A low temperature system will gain a lot of entropy for the same gain in heat. Therefore, since the second law dictates that the entropy in the universe tends to increase, heat is likely to flow from high temperature to low temperature because that leads to a rise in entropy on the whole. Heat flow (except for microscopic random fluctuations) will end when the entropy lost/gained for a loss/gain of heat becomes equal for two systems, which means the total entropy no longer increases when heat flows. This means the two systems are at equal temperatures.

This is rather obvious in the intuitive case of heat transfer. But something similar can be seen in the case of a paramagnet, which gives a very non-intuitive picture of entropy.

Aside: Clausius' inequality evaluates the heat transfer relative to the temperature of the boundary where the heat exchange occurs during a cyclic process:

\[\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0\]

For a process between two distinct states, this manifests as \(dS \ge \frac{\delta Q}{T}\). (More on this later).

docs.title: Paramagnets, Entropy & Temperature
docs.text:
Consider a paramagnetic substance under the influence of an external magnetic field. The individual atoms in the substance act like dipoles: they either align up i.e. in the direction of the magnetic field, or down i.e. in the opposite direction. Let us say the system starts off in the state where all dipoles are aligned with the magnetic field. This is a state with multiplicity \(1\) and therefore, entropy of \(0\). But its potential energy \(U\) is at the minimum. This state is called lower lockout.

If we were to add energy to the system, the dipoles would begin to flip their orientation into the higher potential energy state where they oppose the magnetic field orientation. The multiplicity of the states that the system begins to occupy also increases as more atoms begin to flip. So the system is absorbing energy and its entropy is increasing, which means it starts to have a positive temperature.

Eventually, half the atoms will be flipped and half will be aligned with the magnetic field. This is a state of maximum multiplicity and entropy. The entropy cannot increase beyond this even with the addition of energy and this state is called saturation. Since the statistical definition of temperature is \(\frac{1}{T} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\), \(T\) goes to infinity as the slope \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\) goes to \(0\). Now let's say we continue to add more energy to the system. More atoms will continue to flip, but now the entropy begins to decrease. This means the slope \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\) becomes negative, so \(T\) jumps to negative infinity. As energy continues to be added, entropy drops faster and faster, which means \(T\) remains negative but approaches \(0\) from below, and eventually reaches \(0\) again in the case where every atom is flipped, a state with multiplicity \(1\). This state is called upper lockout.

In fact, if we were to take a system at a very low positive temperature (where almost all atoms are aligned with the magnetic field) and suddenly reverse the magnetic field's orientation, the atoms are instantly left anti-aligned with the new field. This places the system immediately into a high-energy, low-entropy state, which is a negative temperature. The atoms would then begin to relax and flip to align with the new field direction, releasing a tremendous amount of energy as their entropy rises and the temperature approaches negative infinity, flips to positive infinity, and cools back down.

The temperature referenced in the spin system is the thermodynamic temperature, which is related to energy and entropy. This need not be the same as what we traditionally call "hot" and "cold", which is a specific manifestation of thermodynamic temperature known as kinetic temperature—it arises from the kinetic and translational movement of atoms and molecules.

If we graphed the spin system with entropy on the y-axis and the number of particles in a certain spin state (which is proportional to internal energy \(U\)) on the x-axis, the plot would be a parabolic arch.

The left end near the origin would have a positive \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\), so this state would be ready to absorb massive amounts of energy. The right side would have a negative \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\) and would be ready to release massive amounts of energy, though it is at a "negative temperature" or rather because it is at a negative temperature. The top of the graph would be flat and represent the maximum entropy and therefore infinite temperatures.

Note that this behaviour of negative temperatures is possible only because our system has an upper bound on energy and entropy. In general, in classical mechanics, the energy and entropy curves extend infinitely to the right and never reach a maximum peak or turn downward.

In solid-state physics, a material effectively contains two independent thermodynamic systems occupying the exact same physical space: 1. The Lattice: The physical structure of vibrating atoms. This unbounded system has a standard kinetic temperature. 2. The Spin System: The localized magnetic moments. This bounded system has its own independent thermodynamic temperature based strictly on the spin multiplicity.

Because the coupling (energy exchange) between the electron or nuclear spins and the physical lattice is often extremely weak, these two systems can be out of equilibrium. You can physically hold a crystal where the lattice is at a standard kinetic temperature of \(300\text{ K}\), but by using radio-frequency pulses, you can drive the localized spin system into a population inversion, giving the spin system a negative thermodynamic temperature.

If the bounded spin system were to suddenly couple strongly to the unbounded physical lattice, energy would flow explosively from the negative-temperature spins into the positive-temperature lattice, rapidly heating the physical material until the spin "temperature" and lattice temperature equalized.

docs.title: The First & Second Laws & the Thermodynamic Identity
docs.text:
The first law of thermodynamics states that energy is conserved. In thermodynamics, this means the change in the internal energy of the system is equal to the heat input to the system plus the work done on the system.

\[dU = \delta Q_{ ext{in}} + \delta W_{ ext{onsystem}}\]

This always holds true for any closed system (except if you are looking at the expansion of the universe!).

The second law provides the macroscopic definition of entropy: \(dS = rac{\delta Q_{ ext{rev}}}{T}\) or \(\delta Q_{ ext{rev}} = TdS\).

Mechanical work done on a fluid or gas system during a reversible volume change is:

\[\delta W_{ ext{rev}} = -PdV\]

If we assume a closed system where the number of particles remains constant, we can substitute these into the first law to get:

\[dU = TdS - PdV\]

This is the fundamental thermodynamic identity. This is an equation written entirely in state variables. Therefore, though we derived it for a reversible process, this equation holds for the differential between any two neighbouring equilibrium states, regardless of whether the actual physical process connecting them was reversible or irreversible.

If we are considering an open system where the number of particles can change, the fundamental thermodynamic identity becomes:

\[dU = TdS - PdV + \mu dN\]

where \(\mu\) is the chemical potential and \(N\) is the number of particles in the system.

If the system involves some work other than the mechanical work to change volume, such as electrical work, these should also be included in the first law and the thermodynamic identity. They become:

\[dU = \delta Q - \delta W_{ ext{expansion}} + \delta W_{ ext{elec}}\]

and

\[dU = TdS - PdV + \mu dN + \delta W_{ ext{elec}}\]

Since the thermodynamic identity is generally written as an intensive property multiplied by the differential of an extensive property, this becomes: \(dU = TdS - PdV + \mu dN + \phi dq\)

Note: The thermodynamic identity is a relationship between state variables, meaning it is mathematically valid for evaluating the difference between the endpoints of any process, whether reversible or irreversible, provided the initial and final states are in thermodynamic equilibrium. By equilibrium, we mean uniform intensive variables, i.e. \(T\), \(P\) and \(\mu\) are uniform throughout the system. If the system is not in equilibrium, for example if there are massive temperature gradients, pressure waves, and turbulent vortices throughout the volume, then the system as a whole does not possess a single, globally defined temperature or pressure that can be utilized in the equation. In such cases, we may be able to assume "local thermodynamic equilibrium," where the system is mathematically divided into infinitesimally small volume elements that are treated as being locally in equilibrium, allowing the identity to be applied differentially across spatial gradients.

Note on Pressure: You can isolate the formula for pressure from the fundamental thermodynamic identity (\(dU = TdS - PdV + \mu dN\)). By holding entropy and particle number constant (\(dS = 0\), \(dN = 0\)), you get:

\[P = -\left( rac{\partial U}{\partial V} ight)_{S, N}\]

Pressure is therefore the energy needed to make a unit change in volume.

Note on Chemical Potentials: The chemical potential of a particle can be deduced by analyzing chemical reactions involving that particle in equilibrium. For example, when an electron transitions to a lower energy state, a photon is emitted:

\[e^- ightleftharpoons e^- + \gamma\]

At thermal and chemical equilibrium, the sum of the chemical potentials of the reactants must equal the products:

\[\mu_e = \mu_e + \mu_\gamma\]

Which dictates that \(\mu_\gamma = 0\). Photons in a thermal cavity have a chemical potential of zero because their particle number is not conserved; they can be freely created or destroyed to minimize the free energy of the system.

Similarly, assuming the chemical potential of a neutrino (\( u\)) and its antineutrino (\( ar{ u}\)) are equal (\(\mu_ u = \mu_{ ar{ u}}\)), we can look at their annihilation reaction:

\[ u + ar{ u} ightleftharpoons \gamma\]

This implies:

\[2\mu_ u = \mu_\gamma = 0\]

Which means the chemical potential \(\mu_ u = 0\) for both neutrinos and antineutrinos in thermal equilibrium.

Thus, temperature is the driving potential for heat, pressure for volume and chemical potential for diffusion.

For a system in equilibrium, the internal energy \(U\) can be expressed by the Euler relation:

\[U = TS - PV + \mu N\]

The Euler relation is not independent of the thermodynamic identity. It is a direct mathematical consequence of the fact that \(U\), \(S\), \(V\), and \(N\) are extensive properties.

If you scale the size of a system by a factor of \(\lambda\), all extensive properties scale by that exact same factor. Therefore:

\[U(\lambda S, \lambda V, \lambda N) = \lambda U(S, V, N)\]

In multivariable calculus, a function that behaves this way is called a homogeneous function of degree one. According to Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions, if you differentiate this scaling equation with respect to \(\lambda\) and then set \(\lambda = 1\), the math strictly dictates that:

\[U = TS - PV + \mu N\]

Taking the total differential of this equation yields \(dU = TdS + SdT - PdV - VdP + \mu dN + Nd\mu\). Subtracting the thermodynamic identity from this gives the Gibbs-Duhem relation: $\(SdT - VdP + Nd\mu = 0\)$

This equation serves as a constraint on the intensive properties, i.e. \(T\), \(P\) and \(\mu\) cannot vary independently of each other. If you change any two, the change in the third is already determined.

Now, taking the thermodynamic identity and assuming that the number of particles does not change (\(dN = 0\)), we get:

\[dU = TdS - PdV\]

If the system is quasistatic, meaning any change made to the system is so slow that the system always has time to reach equilibrium after each infinitesimal step, the change will be reversible and we get: \(\delta Q_{ ext{in}} = TdS\) and \(\delta W_{ ext{on}} = -PdV\). Note that these hold true even when there is friction, provided we ignore the work done to overcome friction and the heat lost due to friction to "non-system" components (such as the piston head).

However, consider a non-quasistatic system, for example, one in which a piston is being rapidly compressed on a chamber of gas. The gas particles near the piston will be pushed to a higher pressure than the rest of the gas (since they do not have time to equilibrate), exerting an extra reverse pressure on the piston greater than the average equilibrium pressure of the chamber. Therefore, more force will be required to compress the piston compared to the quasistatic case. Since compression means \(dV\) is negative, \(-PdV\) is a positive value representing the reversible work. The actual work required for the compression will be greater that the quasistatic case, so \(\delta W_{ ext{on}} > -PdV\).

By the Clausius inequality (\(dS \ge rac{\delta Q}{T}\)), the heat input will be \(\delta Q_{ ext{in}} < TdS\).

Therefore, even in a non-quasistatic case, the First Law \(dU = \delta Q_{ ext{in}} + \delta W_{ ext{on}}\) still holds true, but the individual components map to the thermodynamic identity as inequalities: \(\delta Q_{ ext{in}} < TdS\) and \(\delta W_{ ext{on}} > -PdV\). The decreased heat input (or increased heat rejected) is perfectly counterbalanced by the increased work done on the system. Therefore, the thermodynamic identity still holds:

\[dU = TdS - PdV\]

Note that during this rapid compression, the system may not be in equilibrium. The thermodynamic identity can be applied only in systems in equilibrium. However, we can always rapidly compress the gas, and then wait for the system to equilibrate before applying the thermodynamic identity. This is fine since what we are interested in is really the relationship between the initial and final states.

Going back to our formula for entropy, \(dS = rac{\delta Q_{ ext{rev}}}{T}\), we can see that \(\delta Q_{ ext{in}} < \delta Q_{ ext{rev}}\) in the non-quasistatic case. Essentially, if a process is not reversible, we extract less heat from it (or must expel more heat) compared to the reversible case. But the rise in the system's entropy is still dictated by \(\delta Q_{ ext{rev}}\) , so we end up "paying" a penalty of entropy equivalent to the reversible case, even though we extract less useful heat from the process.

docs.title: Enthalpy & Free Energies
docs.text:
Suppose we wanted to calculate the heat released when aviation fuel is burnt in a constant pressure situation. You could build a calorimeter, burn the exact fuel blend, and measure the temperature change. But if the fuel mixture changes slightly tomorrow, you must run the physical experiment again.

Ideally, we would like to have reference tables that tell us how much heat the chemical reaction will release. If we could reduce this to a formula based purely on state variables, we would have a deterministic framework. We could write equations to mix and match various chemicals and figure out how much heat each mixture will release without needing an experiment for every permutation.

From the first law and the thermodynamic identity, \(dU = \delta Q + \delta W_{\text{total}}\). If the only work done is reversible expansion work, then \(\delta W_{\text{total}} = -PdV\), and the heat input (or in the case of the aviation fuel example, the heat output) is \(\delta Q = TdS\).

The trouble with using \(U\) as a state variable is that the heat input to the system provides for the rise in internal energy as well as for the expansion work done to accommodate the system's changing volume. Therefore, \(U\) does not equate to heat input.

Instead, if we had a variable \(H\) (enthalpy) that also included the expansion work, such that:

\[dH = dU + PdV\]

then \(dH = TdS\) which is just the heat input (output).

We therefore define \(H\) as \(U + PV\). Since \(H\) is a state variable, we can look them up via tables and perform the mix and match calculations we want to so that fuels can mixed etc.

Note that taking the differential of this equation results in: \(dH = dU + VdP + PdV\). However, enthalpy is usually utilized in isobaric systems where \(dP = 0\), and this equation reduces to \(dH = dU + PdV\) and therefore to \(dH = \delta Q\) .

Similarly, we can define the Helmholtz Free Energy \(F\) as the total reversible work done on the system when the temperature is constant (thus, the work includes the non-extractable work that was expended by the system in expanding the volume). If we had \(dF = dU - TdS\), then since \(dU = TdS - PdV + \delta W_{on}\), we are left with \(dF = - PdV + \delta W_{on}\) which is the work done on the system (by let's say some electrical system for example) minus the work done by the system in expanding the atmosphere, or whatever other ambient setup, during the process.

We therefore define \(F\) as \(U - TS\). Note that taking the differential of this equation results in: \(dF = dU -TdS -SdT\). However, Helmholtz Free Energy is usually utilized in constant temperature systems and this equation reduces to the previous one.

Next, we define the Gibbs Free Energy \(G\) as the total useful work done on the system, (i.e. the work needed to expand the surrounding medium is not included), when temperature and pressure are constant. If we had \(dG = dH - TdS\), then since \(dH = TdS -PdV + \delta W_{other} + PdV\), we are left with \(dG = W_{other}\) which is exactly the useful work done on the system (by let's say some electrical system for example).

We therefore define \(G\) as \(H - TS\). Note that taking the differential of this equation results in: \(dG = dU + PdV + VdP -TdS -SdT\). However, Gibbs Free Energy is usually utilized in constant temperature and pressure systems and this equation reduces to the previous one.

Legendre Transforms Perspective: Another way of looking at these state variables is through Legendre transformations. The internal energy \(U(S, V, N)\) depends on extensive variables.

  • Enthalpy (\(H\)) is useful for constant-pressure systems, swapping the extensive \(V\) for its intensive conjugate \(P\).
  • Helmholtz Free Energy (\(F\)) is useful for constant-temperature systems, swapping the extensive \(S\) for its intensive conjugate \(T\).
  • Gibbs Free Energy (\(G\)) is useful for systems at constant temperature and pressure (like most chemical reactions), swapping both \(S\) and \(V\) for their intensive conjugates \(T\) and \(P\).

Why the Legendre Transforms are useful? The Second Law of Thermodynamics dictates that an isolated system will spontaneously evolve to maximize its entropy. Consequently, for a system held at constant \(S\) and \(V\), equilibrium is reached when the internal energy \(U\) is minimized.
